title: Celsus’s tale of a revolt from Egypt
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος οἰόμενος τοὺς Ἰουδαίους. Αἰγυπτίους τῷ γένει τυγχάνοντας, καταλελοιπέναι τὴν Αἴγυπτον, στασιάσαντας πρὸς τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων καὶ τὸ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ σύνηθες περὶ τὰς θρησκείας ὑπερφρονήσαντας, φησὶν αὐτοὺς ἅπερ ἐποίησαν Αἰγυπτίοις πεπονθέναι ὑπὸ τῶν προσθεμένων τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ πιστευσάντων αὐτῷ ὡς Χριστῷ, καὶ ἀμφοτέροις αἴτιον γεγονέναι τῆς καινοτομίας τὸ στασιάζειν πρὸς τὸ κοινόν. τί δὴ πεποίηκεν ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ὁ Κέλσος. κατανοητέον. πολλὰ διαθέντες οἱ πάλαι Αἰγύπτιοι τὸ Ἑβραίων γένος, διὰ λιμὸν τὴν Ἰουδαίαν καταλαβόντα ἐπιδημήσαντας τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ. πεπόνθασιν ὡς ξένους καὶ ἱκέτας ἀδικήσαντες ἅπερ ἐχρῆν ὅλον ἔθνος ὑπὸ τῆς θείας προνοίας παθεῖν, συμφρονῆσαν κατὰ ὅλου τοῦ τῶν ἐπιξενωθέντων αὐτοῖς γένους μηδὲν αὐτοὺς ἀδικήσαντος· καὶ θεοῦ μάστιξιν πληγέντες μόλις καὶ μετ᾿ οὐ πολὺ ἀπέλυσαν ὅποι ἐβούλοντο τοὺς Οὐ δικαίως δουλαγωγουμένους. ἅτε οὖν φίλαυτοι καὶ τοὺς ὁποιωσδήποτε ὁμογενεῖς προτιμῶντες καὶ τῶν δικαιοτέρων ξένων, οὐχ ἔστιν ἥντινα κατηγορίαν καταλελοίπασιν, ἣν μὴ περὶ Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν Ἑβραίων εἰρήκασι, τὰς μὲν διὰ Μωϋσέως τεραστίους δυνάμεις οὐ παντελῶς ἀρνούμενοι φάσκοντες δ᾿ αὐτὰς γοητείᾳ καὶ μὴ θείᾳ δύνάμει γεγονέναι. Μωϋσῆς δὲ [τὰ συμβεβηκότα] ὡς οὐ γόης ἀλλ᾿ εὐσεβὴς ἀνὴρ καὶ τῷ τῶν ὅλων ἀνακείμενος θεῷ καὶ μετέχων θειοτέρου πνεύματος καὶ νόμους ἔθετο τοῖς Ἑβραίοις. ὡς τὸ θεῖον αὐτῷ ὑπήχησε, καὶ τὰ συμβεβηκότα, ὡς ἀληθείας εἶχεν, ἀνέγραψεν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus, thinking that the Jews, being Egyptians by race (γένος), left (καταλείπω) Egypt, having revolted (στασιάζω) against the commonwealth (τὸ κοινόν) of the Egyptians and having despised (ὑπερφρονέω) the custom (σύνηθες) in Egypt about religious rites (θρησκεία), says that they have suffered from those who attached themselves (προστίθεμαι) to Jesus and believed in him as Christ the very things they did to the Egyptians, and that for both the cause (αἴτιον) of the innovation (καινοτομία) was revolting against the commonwealth. What Celsus has done in the passage (τόπος) must be observed (κατανοητέον). The Egyptians of old, having treated (διατίθημι) the race of the Hebrews badly in many ways, [the Hebrews] having sojourned (ἐπιδημέω) in Egypt because of a famine (λιμός) that seized (καταλαμβάνω) Judaea, suffered, having wronged (ἀδικέω) them as strangers (ξένος) and suppliants (ἱκέτης), what a whole nation had to suffer from divine providence (πρόνοια), having conspired (συμφρονέω) against the whole race of those received as guests (ἐπιξενόομαι) by them, which had wronged them in nothing; and struck (πλήσσω) by God’s scourges (μάστιξ) barely (μόλις) and after not long (μετ᾿ οὐ πολύ) they released (ἀπολύω) wherever they wished those unjustly (οὐ δικαίως) enslaved (δουλαγωγέω). Being then self-loving (φίλαυτος) and preferring (προτιμάω) those of the same race (ὁμογενής), of whatever sort, even to more just (δικαιότερος) strangers, there is no accusation (κατηγορία) they have left which they have not said about Moses and the Hebrews, not altogether denying (ἀρνέομαι) the wondrous (τεράστιος) powers through Moses but saying (φάσκω) they came about by sorcery (γοητεία) and not by divine power (θεία δύναμις). But Moses, as not a sorcerer (γόης) but a pious (εὐσεβής) man, dedicated (ἀνάκειμαι) to the God of the universe and sharing (μετέχω) a more divine spirit (θειότερον πνεῦμα), both laid down laws (νόμους τίθημι) for the Hebrews as the divine (τὸ θεῖον) prompted (ὑπηχέω) him, and recorded (ἀναγράφω) the things that happened (τὰ συμβεβηκότα) as they held of truth (ὡς ἀληθείας εἶχεν).
pass_b_english: Next, Celsus supposes that the Jews, being Egyptians by race, left Egypt after rising in revolt against the Egyptian commonwealth and scorning the religious customs of Egypt. He says that what they did to the Egyptians they have suffered at the hands of those who joined Jesus and believed in him as Christ, and that in both cases the cause of the new movement was revolt against the commonwealth.

We must consider what Celsus has done here. The Egyptians of old treated the race of the Hebrews badly in many ways (Exodus 1:11–14), after the Hebrews had come to dwell in Egypt because of a famine that had seized Judaea (Genesis 47:4). For wronging strangers and suppliants they suffered what a whole nation was bound to suffer at the hands of divine providence, since it had conspired against the whole race of its guests, who had done it no wrong. Struck by scourges from God, they let go, grudgingly, though before long, those whom they were unjustly holding in slavery, to go wherever they wished (Exodus 12:31–32).

Since, then, the Egyptians love themselves and prefer their own countrymen, whatever they are like, even to foreigners who are more just, there is no accusation they have failed to make against Moses and the Hebrews. They do not altogether deny the wonderful works done through Moses, but they say these were done by sorcery and not by divine power. Moses, however, being no sorcerer but a devout man, dedicated to the God of the universe and sharing in a more divine spirit, both laid down laws for the Hebrews as God prompted him and recorded what had happened just as it truly was.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 5 (Koetschau 3.5). Celsus’s charge is reported in indirect speech (infinitives) and is left without quotation marks. ‘τὸ κοινόν’ rendered ‘the commonwealth’ (the common body of the Egyptians here; of the Jews in 3.7, where the same word is used so that Origen’s echo of Celsus’s phrase stays visible). The famine and the sojourn follow the Joseph story (Genesis 47:4, ‘we have come to sojourn in the land … for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan’); Origen calls the land ‘Judaea’ by the name of his own day. The ill-treatment is Exodus 1:11–14; the release after the plagues is Exodus 12:31–32. ‘μόλις καὶ μετ᾿ οὐ πολύ’ is difficult: literally ‘with difficulty and after no long time’; rendered ‘grudgingly, though before long’, following the staged copy-text as it stands (the pairing is awkward; checked against the Greek only, no emendation adopted). The staged text has ‘Οὐ δικαίως’ with a stray capital; read as ‘οὐ δικαίως’ (unjustly). The bracketed ‘[τὰ συμβεβηκότα]’ after ‘Μωϋσῆς δὲ’ is an editorial deletion (the phrase recurs at the end) and is translated only once, in its proper place. ‘ὡς τὸ θεῖον αὐτῷ ὑπήχησε’: τὸ θεῖον (‘the Divine’) refers to God and is rendered ‘as God prompted him’. ‘θειοτέρου πνεύματος’ is comparative and general (‘a more divine spirit’), so it is not capitalised. The Egyptian accusers (perfect tenses καταλελοίπασιν, εἰρήκασι) are the Egyptian writers on Moses; no names are given in the Greek and none are supplied. ‘τῶν δικαιοτέρων ξένων’ rendered ‘foreigners who are more just’ (the comparative has no expressed object, so ‘than they’ is not added). No LXX renumbering arises.
τὸ κοινόν made ‘commonwealth’ in both places (was ‘state’), to fit both the Egyptians and, in 3.7, the Jews
inline citations moved beside their clauses: Exodus 1:11–14 by the ill-treatment, Genesis 47:4 by the famine and sojourn
‘what a whole nation had to suffer’ made ‘was bound to suffer’ (ἐχρῆν, necessity, not mere occurrence)
‘reluctantly and yet before long’ made ‘grudgingly, though before long’ (μόλις); unverified note about an emendation removed
‘more righteous than they’ made ‘who are more just’ (no ‘than they’ in the Greek)
Exodus 12:31–32 checked: Pharaoh lets the people go after the plagues; correct
